debate_title: Should AI developers be legally liable for harms caused b...

conflicts.point: Whether downstream fine-tuning and parameter adjustments fundamentally sever the causal chain of liability from foundational model developers to end-use operators.

positions.stance: Downstream fine-tuning and quantization alter parameters so radically that the original upstream model is functionally transformed, making foundational creators an improper target for tort liability.
Base training runs establish immutable capability ceilings and behavioral attractors that downstream fine-tuning cannot strip out, maintaining causal responsibility upstream.

conflicts.point: Whether attaching strict tort liability to foundational code creators protects consumers or instead establishes a regulatory moat that entrenches cloud oligopolies and crushes decentralized open-weight distribution.

positions.stance: Strict upstream liability imposes compliance costs that only large cloud oligopolies can absorb, thereby destroying decentralized open-source innovation and locking out small startups.
Holding commercial foundational vendors accountable establishes necessary baseline product safety without harming academic or open-source research.

verdicts.conflict: Whether downstream fine-tuning and parameter adjustments fundamentally sever the causal chain of liability from foundational model developers to end-use operators.
verdicts.rationale: Neither side presents conclusive empirical benchmarks to prove whether base model attractors override fine-tuning or if quantization completely rewrites behavioral boundaries. Both claims rely on competing analogies about software architecture rather than standardized forensic testing of modified weights.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Controlled technical audits of fine-tuned models tracking how often harmful outputs stem from upstream pre-training versus downstream modification would tip the balance.

verdicts.conflict: Whether attaching strict tort liability to foundational code creators protects consumers or instead establishes a regulatory moat that entrenches cloud oligopolies and crushes decentralized open-weight distribution.
verdicts.rationale: The accelerationist position offers a more concrete mechanism by linking unbounded tort exposure directly to compliance overhead and startup attrition. The skeptic counter-argument correctly notes existing market concentration by cloud providers, but fails to demonstrate how adding strict liability would prevent oligopolies from simply absorbing the legal risk while crushing smaller open-source competitors.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Empirical studies showing that open-source developers can successfully insure against strict liability risks without prohibitive cost increases would reverse this finding.
